---
title: "Data Representations"
---

`sblr` can fit Bayesian linear regression models from two broad forms of
genomic data:

1. **individual-level data**, where marker genotypes and phenotypes are
   available for the same individuals; and
2. **summary statistics plus linkage disequilibrium (LD)**, where the sampler
   receives cross-products that summarize the genotype-phenotype data rather
   than the full observed matrices.

These are two representations of closely related regression calculations, not
two unrelated model families. The representation determines what must be
stored, what can be recomputed during sampling, and which alignment and
sample-overlap assumptions must be made explicit.

## Individual-Level PLINK BED Representation

Let $X$ be an $n \times m$ genotype matrix for $n$ individuals and $m$
markers, and let $Y$ be an $n \times n_t$ phenotype matrix for $n_t$
traits. For one trait, $Y$ reduces to a vector $y$. A Bayesian linear
regression model can be written as

$$
Y = XB + E,
$$

where $B$ contains marker effects and $E$ contains residuals. In a
single-trait model, this is $y = Xb + e$.

With individual-level data, a marker update can read the observed genotype
column $x_j$ and evaluate quantities such as

$$
x_j^\top x_j
\quad\text{and}\quad
x_j^\top e
=
x_j^\top(y-Xb).
$$

The sampler can therefore update effects from observed marker values and
current individual-level residuals. It does not need a separately supplied LD
matrix because correlations among markers are implicit in $X$.

PLINK BED files store genotype calls compactly on disk rather than as an
in-memory numeric matrix. In the package workflow, a qgg `Glist` supplies the
BED file paths and related metadata:

- `Glist$bedfiles` identifies the BED files;
- `Glist$n` gives the number of individuals;
- `Glist$rsids` identifies the marker columns in each BED file;
- `Glist$af` or `Glist$maf` supplies allele frequencies or MAF used when
  markers are standardized or when MAF-dependent priors are used;
- `Glist$rsidsLD` identifies the selected markers and their intended LD order.

`stblr_bed()` is the high-level direct BED interface. It receives the `Glist`,
phenotype vector or matrix `y`, optional chromosome selection, and optional
marker column indices `cls`. Its BED samplers read marker blocks from disk and
perform marker updates without first materializing all of $X$ or a full
$X^\top X$ matrix. Optional `rows` select 1-based individual indices, and
`scale = TRUE` standardizes markers using the corresponding allele
frequencies. `stblr_bed_marker()` remains available as a lower-level BED marker
interface.

The individual-level representation is information-rich: if the same
individuals have multiple measured traits, cross-trait phenotype and residual
cross-products can be calculated directly. Its main costs are access to
sensitive individual-level data and repeated genotype reading during model
fitting.

## Dense Summary-Statistic Representation

The Gaussian linear model likelihood and marker-update calculations can be
expressed using cross-products. For one trait, the central quantities are

$$
wy = X^\top y,
\qquad
XX = X^\top X,
\qquad
yy = y^\top y,
$$

together with the sample size $n$. For multiple traits,

$$
WY = X^\top Y
$$

contains one marker-trait cross-product column per trait.

The matrix $X^\top X$ describes both marker sums of squares on its diagonal
and marker-marker LD in its off-diagonal entries. In package interfaces,
`ww` denotes per-trait marker sums of squares or corresponding diagonal
information, while LD supplies the off-diagonal relationships needed to
propagate an effect update to correlated markers. Depending on scaling and
the producing function, LD may be represented in correlation units or as the
corresponding genotype cross-products. The statistics and LD representation
must use the same marker scaling and order.

These quantities are sufficient for many marker updates because the current
marker-residual score can be represented as

$$
r = X^\top(y-Xb) = wy - X^\top Xb.
$$

If marker $j$'s effect changes by $\Delta b_j$, the updated score can be
calculated from column $j$ of $X^\top X$:

$$
r_{\text{new}}
=
r_{\text{old}} - (X^\top X)_{\cdot j}\Delta b_j.
$$

This is why a summary-statistics sampler needs more than marginal
genotype-phenotype associations. It needs enough information to reproduce the
cross-products used by the marker-update and variance calculations. Marginal
`wy` values without compatible LD cannot account for correlated markers, and
LD without `wy`, `yy`, and $n$ does not define the phenotype side of the
likelihood.

A dense representation stores all of $X^\top X$, which requires
$O(m^2)$ entries. That becomes impractical for large marker sets. The
disk-backed sparse-LD representation retains the same conceptual role while
dropping small or distant marker-marker entries.

## Disk-Backed CSR Sparse-LD Representation

Compressed sparse row (CSR) format stores only retained entries of a sparse
matrix. Conceptually, it records:

- a vector of row pointers delimiting each matrix row;
- column indices for retained entries; and
- the retained LD or cross-product values.

`sparseLD_stream_CSR()` computes sparse LD directly from one or more PLINK BED
files and writes a disk-backed CSR representation at `out_prefix`. The
selected marker columns are supplied as a list through `cls`, one vector per
BED file. Optional `rows` and `af` must describe the same individuals and
marker scaling used for the sufficient statistics.

Sparsification is controlled by:

- `r2_threshold`, which removes pairs below a squared-correlation threshold;
- `max_distance_bp`, which can restrict pairs by base-pair distance;
- `max_distance_variants`, which can restrict pairs by marker-index distance;
- `block_size` and `nthreads`, which control construction rather than the
  statistical definition.

The sparse representation approximates $X^\top X$. It reduces memory and
disk requirements when most long-range or weak marker relationships can be
ignored, but the threshold and distance rules become part of the analysis.
Two fits using different sparse-LD construction rules do not have identical
inputs even if they began from the same BED file.

`sparseLD_read_CSR()` reads files written by `sparseLD_stream_CSR()` and
returns row pointers, column indices, and values. Its `one_based` option
controls the indexing convention of returned column indices. This reader is
useful for checking dimensions, indexing, and retained entries; `stblr_csr()`
uses the disk-backed prefix directly.

Detailed storage and construction contracts belong in
[Technical sparse LD and CSR](technical_sparse_ld_csr.qmd).

## Sufficient Statistics: `wy`, `ww`, and `yy`

`make_summary_stats()` is the package bridge from a BED-backed `Glist` and phenotypes
to the sufficient statistics consumed by `stblr_csr()`. It resolves BED files,
selected chromosomes, selected BED marker columns `cls`, allele frequencies,
phenotype-to-BED row matching, and marker names from `Glist`. Optional `rows`
and `scale` determine which individuals and marker standardization are used.
The lower-level `bed_xtx_xty()` helper performs per-BED cross-product work.

The returned `stats` object contains the marker-trait cross-products and
related quantities required by the ST-BLR wrapper:

- `stats$wy`: $X^\top Y$, represented by trait;
- `stats$ww`: marker sums of squares or diagonal genotype cross-product
  information, represented by trait;
- `stats$yy`: $y_t^\top y_t$ for each trait;
- `stats$n` and `stats$m`, when available, for sample and marker counts.

`make_sparse_ld()` computes disk-backed sparse LD from the same BED-backed
`Glist` and stores the resulting CSR prefix and resolved marker metadata in
`Glist$sparseLD`. This metadata includes the sparse-LD prefix, marker order,
selected BED columns, rows, allele frequencies, distance limits, threshold,
and construction settings used by CSR models. `stblr_csr()` combines `stats`
with this sparse-LD metadata from `Glist`, or with an explicit `ld_prefix`
when supplied. The wrapper
initializes per-trait variance quantities using `stats$yy`, $n$, and $m$, then
passes `wy`, `ww`, `yy`, and the CSR prefix to the sparse-LD sampler.

The complete conceptual bridge is:

```text
BED files + aligned phenotypes
          |
          +--> make_summary_stats() ---------> wy, ww, yy, n, marker names
          |
          +--> make_sparse_ld() ------> Glist$sparseLD prefix and metadata
                                        |
                                        v
                        stblr_csr() summary-statistics model
```

The two branches must be produced from the same marker selection, sample
selection, allele frequencies, and scaling convention. In contrast,
`stblr_bed()` follows a direct branch from BED files and phenotypes to the
individual-level sampler. The worked comparison is described in
[Sparse-LD and BED workflows](sparse_ld_and_bed_workflows.qmd).

## Multi-Trait Cross-Products, Sample Overlap, and `SSY`

The phrase "multi-trait summary statistics" can refer to two different levels
of information.

First, traits can be fitted as separate or parallel single-trait regressions.
For trait $t$, the phenotype sum of squares is

$$
yy_t = y_t^\top y_t = \sum_i y_{it}^2.
$$

A vector of `yy` values, with corresponding columns of $X^\top Y$, is enough
to initialize and fit per-trait likelihood calculations that do not require
observed cross-trait phenotype products. The current `stblr_csr()` wrapper
uses this per-trait representation: it infers the number of traits from
`length(stats$yy)` and uses each `yy_t` to initialize trait-specific
variances.

Second, a genuinely joint multi-trait likelihood with a full residual
covariance matrix requires the cross-trait phenotype matrix

$$
\mathrm{SSY} = Y^\top Y,
\qquad
\mathrm{SSY}_{ts}
=
\sum_{i \in \mathcal I_{ts}} y_{it}y_{is},
$$

where $\mathcal I_{ts}$ is the set of individuals observed for both traits.
The diagonal entries are the univariate `yy_t`; the off-diagonal entries
contain information that a vector of `yy` values does not preserve.

With individual-level $Y$, `SSY` and the effective overlap counts can be
calculated from observed individuals. With summary statistics, they must be
provided or reconstructed. If $N_{ts}$ is the number of individuals shared
by traits $t$ and $s$, and $R_y$ is a phenotypic correlation matrix, a
common approximation is

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{SSY}}
=
N \odot \widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}(Y),
$$

with diagonals forced to the observed `yy_t`. This approximation assumes that
overlap counts and phenotypic covariance information are meaningful for the
study design. Full overlap, partial overlap, missingness, and meta-analysis
can imply materially different $N$ matrices.

Without cross-trait `SSY` and overlap information, a summary-statistics model
cannot reconstruct the cross-products needed for full residual covariance
updates. The complete derivation and assumptions are preserved in
[Technical multi-trait sample overlap](technical_multitrait_overlap.qmd).

## Marker Ordering and Annotation Alignment

Marker order is a correctness condition, not presentation metadata. Every
marker-indexed object must refer to the same biological marker at position
$j$:

```text
BED marker column selected by cls
    = Glist$rsidsLD marker j
    = sufficient-statistic row j
    = sparse-LD row and column j
    = annotation-matrix row j
    = posterior-summary row j
```

In the workflows, the intended LD marker order is established by
`Glist$rsidsLD[[chr]]`. The BED column indices are derived with

```r
cls <- match(Glist$rsidsLD[[chr]], Glist$rsids[[chr]])
stopifnot(!anyNA(cls))
```

The same `cls` is then supplied to `make_summary_stats()` and `make_sparse_ld()`.
Allele frequencies or MAF are subset with the same indices:

```r
maf_ld <- Glist$maf[[chr]][match(Glist$rsidsLD[[chr]], Glist$rsids[[chr]])]
```

Do not use `%in%` for this alignment because it tests membership but does not
preserve the requested LD/model order.
For annotation models, the $m \times K$ annotation matrix `A` must have one
row per selected marker in exactly this order. The annotation workflow makes
that contract explicit by assigning `Glist$rsidsLD[[chr]]` as row names and
checking that they are identical to the expected marker IDs.

Posterior matrices such as `fit$bm` and `fit$dm` inherit the marker ordering
used by the model input. A plausible-looking result is still invalid if its
rows are joined to annotations or marker metadata in a different order.

Sample alignment is equally important. When `rows` is used, the phenotype
rows and every BED-derived object must describe the same individuals.
Sufficient statistics generated from one sample subset cannot be combined
with sparse LD generated from another without changing the implied model.

## Representation-Specific Limitations and Validation Checks

Individual-level and summary-statistics representations have different
failure modes.

**Individual-level BED fitting**

- requires access to individual genotypes and aligned phenotypes;
- reads genotype blocks repeatedly during fitting;
- can calculate observed phenotype and residual cross-products when data are
  jointly available;
- still requires correct `cls`, `rows`, allele frequencies, and scaling.

**Summary statistics plus sparse LD**

- can avoid repeated access to individual-level genotypes after preparation;
- replaces the full $X^\top X$ matrix with an explicit LD approximation;
- requires compatible `wy`, `ww`, `yy`, $n$, and LD;
- requires `SSY` and overlap information for full joint multi-trait residual
  covariance calculations;
- cannot recover information omitted during summarization or sparsification.

At minimum, validate the following before fitting:

1. `cls` contains no missing marker matches and has the expected length.
2. Allele frequencies correspond to the selected marker columns.
3. `make_summary_stats()` and `make_sparse_ld()` use identical marker order, sample
   rows, and scaling choices.
4. CSR dimensions and indexing are consistent with the number of markers.
5. Annotation rows and marker/group vectors use the same marker order.
6. `stats$wy`, `stats$ww`, and posterior marker matrices have compatible
   dimensions.
7. Trait names, `stats$yy`, and phenotype columns are aligned.
8. Multi-trait summary analyses state how `SSY` and sample overlap were
   observed, assumed, or reconstructed.

Comparing posterior summaries from `stblr_bed()` and `stblr_csr()` on the same
prepared data is a useful integration check, but exact numerical agreement is
not expected automatically. Sparse-LD approximation, scaling, sampler
scheduling, finite MCMC error, and prior settings can all affect the
comparison.

Phase 17J records canonical `marker_metadata`, scale, source, and sample
provenance on `make_summary_stats()` and `make_sparse_ld()` outputs for strict
public `mtblr_csr()` validation.
Phase 17K distinguishes block-eigen construction from runtime representation:
the runtime operator is a float-packed reconstructed dense matrix per block,
with mappings and a separate double view of the packed diagonal.
# Internal multivariate block-filtered representation

The internal MT block-eigen route borrows one packed filtered block operator per trait and consumes the matching builder-transformed summary vector. Hard truncation projects `wy`; ridge modes do not. This remains an internal numerical representation.

# Public multivariate block-filtered representation

`mtblr_block_eigen()` exposes the same canonical representation only for
same-BED/by-construction summaries. Runtime storage is reconstructed dense
blocks, not low-rank factors; returned `wy` is the transformed value consumed
by the sampler.

# Planned individual-level MT representation

Phase 17N selects one move-only `PackedBedMatrix`, the existing immutable
`BedPackedGenotypeView`, column-major `n x nt` phenotype/residual matrices, and
one reusable decoded double marker. Phase 17O implements that representation
internally. Only marker-space `X'Y` and final `X'R` enter `mtblr_raw`; the
sample residual and genetic-value matrices remain core-owned and unreturned.
## Public individual-level multivariate BED data

`mtblr_bed()` uses one shared packed BED genotype owner internally and one
complete aligned phenotype matrix. Phenotypes are centered by default but not
scaled; genotypes are standardized from required selected allele frequencies.
Sample residuals and genetic-value matrices remain internal, while ordinary MT
raw `wy` and `r` are marker-space `X'Y` and final `X'R`.

Future multichain MT BED execution will keep one immutable packed owner and one
prepared phenotype/marker representation. Only mutable chain state, residual,
workspace, RNG, and result accumulators scale with live workers or chain count.
Phase 17Q documents this representation but does not implement it.

Phase 17R now implements it internally: packed bytes, Y, maps, X'Y, and order
exist once; each live chain owns only mutable Gibbs state, residual, decoded
marker workspace, RNG, traces, and accumulators. Compact retained records never
duplicate shared preparation data.

Phase 17S exposes compact chains on request. Public memory metadata continues
to count packed bytes, phenotype, maps, marker X'Y, and order exactly once.

Future formal diagnostics use a separate quantity-major, chain/iteration
ordered post-burn trace bundle. It is not a compact chain object and contains
no packed genotype data.
## Internal convergence traces

Phase 17U adds an internal quantity-by-chain-by-iteration Tier 1 bundle,
represented in R as an `nit × nchains × (3*nt)` array. It contains post-burn
B/G/E diagonals only and is independent of compact retained chains.
